full_citation: An, J., Huang, D., Lin, C., & Tai, M. (2025). Measuring gender and racial biases in large language models: Intersectional evidence from automated resume evaluation. PNAS Nexus, 4(3), pgaf089.
models_or_system: GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Flash, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama 3-70b
population_categories: US; gender x race (Black/White and others) via randomized social identities
manipulation: Randomized applicant identities on otherwise comparable entry-level resumes
outcome: Assessment score; implied hiring probability at a threshold
main_result: Higher scores for female candidates; lower scores for Black male candidates; ~1-3 pp differences in hiring probability at a threshold; direction/magnitude vary by model
limitations: US race/gender only; name-based identity; no nationality or religion
relation_to_project: Template for large-scale independent scoring and for translating score gaps into threshold-based interview gaps; supports reporting both score and interview decision
novelty_threat_reason: Different construct (US race/gender), no national-origin or Arab categories

full_citation: An, H., Acquaye, C., Wang, C., Li, Z., & Rudinger, R. (2024). Do large language models discriminate in hiring decisions on the basis of race, ethnicity, and gender? In Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the ACL (Volume 2: Short Papers), 386-397.
population_categories: US; race/ethnicity (White, Hispanic, others) x gender via first names
manipulation: Applicant first name in templated prompts asking the LLM to write an acceptance or rejection email
outcome: Probability of generating an acceptance vs rejection email
main_result: Many settings favour White over Hispanic applicants; masculine White names highest and masculine Hispanic names lowest acceptance; comparative rates vary across templates (idiosyncratic, prompt-sensitive)
limitations: Name-only signal; no CV content; US groups only
relation_to_project: Warns that group rankings are prompt-sensitive: supports fixed, versioned templates and robustness across prompt conditions

full_citation: Armstrong, L., Liu, A., MacNeil, S., & Metaxa, D. (2024). The Silicon Ceiling: Auditing GPT's race and gender biases in hiring. In Proceedings of the 4th ACM Conference on Equity and Access in Algorithms, Mechanisms, and Optimization (EAAMO '24), 1-18.
population_categories: US; 4 racial groups x 2 genders via 32 names; plus 2 'anonymous' controls
manipulation: Name at top of resume (Study 1 assessment); name-conditioned resume generation (Study 2)
sample_size: Study 1: 320 resumes x 3 prompts x 50 trials = 48,000 scores; Study 2: 320 generated resumes
outcome: Overall rating, willingness to interview, hireability scores; coded content of generated resumes
main_result: Some stereotype-consistent biases in scoring; generated resumes for Asian and Hispanic names carried immigrant markers (non-native English, non-US education/work)
limitations: Single model; 'anonymous' controls behaved inconsistently and were dropped from analysis
relation_to_project: (1) Used 50 repeated trials analysed with name as a random effect: precedent for treating repetitions as within-stimulus; (2) anonymous controls were unstable: warns our not_stated control is not a neutral baseline; (3) models link origin to non-native language: supports holding languages constant

full_citation: Gaebler, J. D., Goel, S., Huq, A. Z., & Tambe, P. B. (2024). Auditing large language models for race & gender disparities: Implications for artificial intelligence-based hiring. Behavioral Science & Policy, 10(2), 46-55.
venue: Behavioral Science & Policy (print Oct 2024; online Mar 2025)
url_doi_arxiv: https://doi.org/10.1177/23794607251320229 (preprint arXiv:2404.03086, 'Auditing the Use of Language Models to Guide Hiring Decisions')
models_or_system: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Mistral 7B, Mixtral 8x7B, Claude Instant, Claude 2, Claude 3 Haiku, Claude 3 Sonnet (arXiv version)
population_categories: US; race (White, Black, Hispanic, Asian) x gender via names and pronouns
manipulation: Real K-12 teaching applications edited to signal demographics via names/pronouns (correspondence design)
main_result: Moderate disparities, models slightly favouring women and non-White candidates; robust to prompt variants incl. an added EEOC anti-discrimination statement (robustness run on GPT-3.5); blinding names had little effect; LLMs infer demographics from blinded materials
limitations: Single application domain; robustness checks on one model; correspondence method audits only the manipulated channel
relation_to_project: Anti-discrimination instruction did not remove disparities: sets expectation for our neutrality condition; direction can reverse relative to human audits (post-training): pre-register two-sided tests
novelty_threat_reason: Race/gender in US teaching hires; no national origin

full_citation: Wilson, K., & Caliskan, A. (2024). Gender, race, and intersectional bias in resume screening via language model retrieval. Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society, 7, 1578-1590.
models_or_system: Massive Text Embedding (MTE) retrieval models (cosine similarity), not generative scoring
population_categories: US; race (Black/White) x gender via names
manipulation: Names added to real resumes; retrieval against job descriptions
main_result: White-associated names favoured in 85.1% of cases; Black males disadvantaged in up to 100% of cases. ERRATUM (arXiv v3, 29 Aug 2026): a code bug inverted the gender-only results (reported male preference is female preference and vice versa); race and intersectional results unaffected and replicated by a Salzburg team
limitations: Embedding retrieval rather than instruction-following LLM; published gender results inverted per erratum
relation_to_project: Cite only race/intersectional findings and the erratum; shows name corpus frequency and document length affect outcomes: supports holding length/format constant across clones

full_citation: Iso, H., Pezeshkpour, P., Bhutani, N., & Hruschka, E. (2025). Evaluating bias in LLMs for job-resume matching: Gender, race, and education. In Proceedings of NAACL 2025 (Volume 3: Industry Track), 672-683.
population_categories: US/English; gender, race, educational background
manipulation: Attribute perturbations in job-resume matching
main_result: Recent models reduced bias on explicit gender/race attributes; implicit bias related to educational background remains significant
relation_to_project: Recent models may show small explicit-attribute effects; supports equivalence-style reporting and holding education constant (German institutions across clones)

full_citation: Veldanda, A. K., Grob, F., Thakur, S., Pearce, H., Tan, B., Karri, R., & Garg, S. (2023). Are Emily and Greg still more employable than Lakisha and Jamal? Investigating algorithmic hiring bias in the era of ChatGPT. arXiv:2310.05135. [Workshop version: 'Investigating Hiring Bias in Large Language Models', NeurIPS 2023 R0-FoMo Workshop.]
venue: arXiv preprint; NeurIPS 2023 R0-FoMo workshop (different title)
population_categories: US; gender, race, maternity status, pregnancy status, political affiliation
manipulation: Protected attributes (e.g., names) on otherwise identical resumes
main_result: LLMs robust across race and gender; differences on pregnancy status and political affiliation
limitations: Preprint/workshop; classification task rather than screening decision
relation_to_project: Null race/gender results in an early audit illustrate task dependence; supports using decision-like outcomes (fit score, interview yes/no, forced choice)

full_citation: Nghiem, H., Prindle, J., Zhao, J., & Daume III, H. (2024). "You gotta be a doctor, Lin": An investigation of name-based bias of large language models in employment recommendations. In Proceedings of EMNLP 2024, 7268-7287.
population_categories: US; race x gender via 320 first names
manipulation: First name in hiring and salary prompts across 40 occupations
main_result: Preference for White female-sounding names; salary recommendations vary by up to 5% between subgroups with identical qualifications
relation_to_project: Large per-group sampling as precedent; salary gap as secondary outcome type (not used by us)

full_citation: Salinas, A., Shah, P., Huang, Y., McCormack, R., & Morstatter, F. (2023). The unequal opportunities of large language models: Examining demographic biases in job recommendations by ChatGPT and LLaMA. In Proceedings of EAAMO '23, 1-15.
population_categories: 20 nationalities (list generated by asking ChatGPT for 'common nationalities'; Jordan is the only Arab country, Pakistan also included) x 2 genders (pronouns); US baseline without nationality
manipulation: Explicit country in prompt ('may have to go back to <COUNTRY>') for a laid-off friend in the US; 3 templates
sample_size: 50 generations per template per nationality-gender combination
main_result: Consistent deviations for Mexican candidates (low-paying jobs, lowest median salary); gendered job recommendations; the no-nationality baseline was itself an outlier
limitations: Job recommendation, not screening; nationality list model-generated and Western-skewed; one Arab country
relation_to_project: Closest precedent for an explicit nationality manipulation in an employment prompt; shows omission baseline is not neutral (supports treating not_stated as descriptive, German as reference); does not examine Arab heterogeneity
novelty_threat_reason: Explicit nationality manipulation, but a single Arab country, a recommendation task and a US setting

full_citation: Wang, Z., Wu, Z., Guan, X., Thaler, M., Koshiyama, A., Lu, S., Beepath, S., Ertekin, E., & Perez-Ortiz, M. (2024). JobFair: A framework for benchmarking gender hiring bias in large language models. In Findings of EMNLP 2024, 3227-3246.
population_categories: Gender
manipulation: Gender counterfactuals on resumes across industries
outcome: Resume scores; Rank After Scoring; impact ratio
main_result: Level bias vs spread (variance) bias; taste-based vs statistical decomposition; 7 of 10 LLMs biased against males in at least one industry; bias invariant to resume content for 8 of 10
relation_to_project: Supports analysing variance (spread) as well as means across nationalities, and using qualification tiers to separate content-dependent from content-invariant bias

full_citation: Wen, A., Patil, T., Saxena, A., Fu, Y., O'Brien, S., & Zhu, K. (2025). FAIRE: Assessing racial and gender bias in AI-driven resume evaluations. arXiv:2504.01420.
population_categories: Race, gender
manipulation: Resumes slightly altered to reflect racial or gender identities
main_result: Every model shows some bias; magnitude and direction vary considerably
relation_to_project: Supports measuring both independent scoring and comparative ranking (our baseline + forced choice)

full_citation: Rozado, D. (2026). Gender and positional biases in LLM-based hiring decisions: Evidence from comparative CV/resume evaluations. PeerJ Computer Science, 12, e3628.
population_categories: Gender (male/female first names; explicit gender field; pronouns)
manipulation: Pairs of profession-matched CVs, each pair shown twice with names swapped; variants with explicit gender field, neutral labels (Candidate A/B), pronouns; isolated rating
sample_size: 30,800 decisions (22 models x 70 professions x 10 job descriptions x 2 orders); 30,690 analysed
main_result: Female-named candidates chosen 56.9% vs 43.1%; adding an explicit gender field increased the female preference; first-listed candidate chosen 63.5% vs 36.5% (21 of 22 models individually significant); isolated ratings showed a negligible gender effect; random temperature U(0,1) per pair, same for both orders
limitations: Gender only; synthetic CVs generated by LLMs
relation_to_project: Strongest support for our quad design (swap attributes and both orders); explicit attribute fields amplify effects (our Nationality line is explicit); pairwise and isolated designs can disagree, so both arms are needed

full_citation: Lippens, L. (2024). Computer says 'no': Exploring systemic bias in ChatGPT using an audit approach. Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans, 2(1), 100054.
venue: Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans
models_or_system: GPT-3.5 (13 June 2023 snapshot) via API; prompts in Dutch
population_categories: Flanders/Belgium; 9 name-signalled groups: Arab, Asian, Black American, Central African, Dutch (reference), Eastern European, Hispanic, Turkish, White American; x gender
manipulation: Validated ethnic names on CVs matched to real VDAB vacancies; nationality field held constant ('Belgian'); isolated prompts (no side-by-side comparison)
main_result: All groups scored below Dutch-named candidates (about -0.96 to -2.42 points); Arab -1.41 (SE 0.21); largest penalty for Eastern Europeans; discrimination ratios at a cutoff of 75: 0.85 Arabs, 0.86 Turks; penalties smaller than human meta-analytic benchmarks; temperature varied between 0 and 1.5 in about two-fifths of prompts
limitations: Single model; 'Arab' pooled as one name group; OLS on scores; name signal confounds origin with name-frequency effects
relation_to_project: Closest European LLM CV-screening precedent including Arab and Turkish applicants; our design differs by manipulating an explicit nationality line (not names), splitting 'Arab' into 22 origins, using a German context and multiple models
novelty_threat_reason: Already shows Arab and Turkish penalties in an LLM European CV audit, so 'LLMs penalise Arab applicants' is not new; within-Arab heterogeneity is untested there

full_citation: Tamkin, A., Askell, A., Lovitt, L., Durmus, E., Joseph, N., Kravec, S., Nguyen, K., Kaplan, J., & Ganguli, D. (2023). Evaluating and mitigating discrimination in language model decisions. arXiv:2312.03689.
population_categories: Age, gender, race
manipulation: Demographics inserted explicitly ('Black male') or implicitly via names into LM-generated decision prompts across 70 scenarios
sample_size: 70 decision scenarios x demographic variants (exact n not recorded here)
outcome: Logit of normalised P(yes) for a yes/no decision
main_result: Positive and negative discrimination in some settings; effects larger for explicit than name-based signals; prompt interventions (e.g., 'illegal to discriminate', 'ignore demographics') substantially reduce discrimination; mixed-effects model with random effects for question type
limitations: Single model; nationality and religion not studied
relation_to_project: Explicit signals give larger effects than names (our explicit Nationality line); supports logprob-based secondary outcome and random effects for stimulus; motivates our neutrality condition

full_citation: Tan, B. C. Z., Khoo, S., Doan, B. N., Liu, Z., Chen, N. F., & Lee, R. K.-W. (2026). Small changes, big impact: Demographic bias in LLM-based hiring through subtle sociocultural markers in anonymised resumes. arXiv:2603.05189 (arXiv comment: EMNLP 2026).
population_categories: Singapore; 4 ethnicities x 2 genders
manipulation: Job-irrelevant sociocultural markers (languages, co-curricular activities, volunteering, hobbies) on anonymised resumes
outcome: 1v1 comparison; score and shortlist (top-score rates); with/without rationale
main_result: Models recover demographics from markers with high F1; favour markers associated with Chinese and Caucasian males; language markers alone suffice to infer ethnicity; asking for explanations may amplify bias
relation_to_project: Justifies holding languages constant across clones (German C2, English C1, no Arabic); our required 'reason' field could interact with bias (explore by condition)
novelty_threat_reason: Ethnicity via proxies in Singapore, not national origin / Arab

full_citation: Leininger, C., Veit, H., Assenmacher, M., & Bender, A. (2026). Fairness beyond anonymization? Demographic leakage in German LLM-generated resumes. arXiv:2609.22188 (BIAS 2026 workshop at ECML PKDD).
venue: arXiv preprint (states acceptance at BIAS 2026 @ ECML PKDD)
population_categories: Germany; gender- and ethnicity-associated names
manipulation: Names varied when generating German resumes from anonymised profiles; downstream leakage classifiers
outcome: Recoverability of demographics from generated, anonymised text
main_result: Gender leakage reliably detectable (subtle German word choice); ethnicity leakage comparatively weak
relation_to_project: German-language LLM hiring context with Qwen3; our CVs are fixed templates, so generation leakage does not apply, but supports rendering CVs deterministically rather than generating per nationality
novelty_threat_reason: Leakage in generation, not screening decisions by nationality

full_citation: Gao, Z., Jiang, W., & Yan, Y. (2026). Can LLMs hire fairly? Racial bias in resume screening. arXiv:2606.28978.
population_categories: US; race, gender
manipulation: Paired-resume method of Kline, Rose & Walters (2022)
main_result: The one 2023-vintage model reproduces a pro-White gap (+2.12 pp); every 2024+ model shows a null gap or a significant pro-Black reversal (up to -3.01 pp); same pattern for gender
relation_to_project: Expect possible reversals and vintage effects: two-sided hypotheses, record exact model ids and dates

full_citation: Karvonen, A., & Marks, S. (2025). Robustly improving LLM fairness in realistic settings via interpretability. arXiv:2506.10922.
models_or_system: GPT-4o, Claude 4 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemma-2 27B, Gemma-3, Mistral-24B
population_categories: US; race (Black/White), gender
manipulation: Names/pronouns and subtle cues (college affiliation); realistic context (company names, careers-page culture text, selectivity constraints); four anti-bias prompts
main_result: Anti-bias prompts reduce bias to near zero in simple settings but fail when realistic context is added (up to 12% interview-rate differences, favouring Black and female candidates); biases invisible in chain-of-thought; affine concept editing reduces bias
relation_to_project: Our neutrality paragraph is tested with minimal job ads (a 'simple setting'): a null after neutrality may not generalise to richer contexts; state this limitation

full_citation: Castleman, J., Shen, Z., Metevier, B., Springer, M., & Korolova, A. (2026). Measuring validity in LLM-based resume screening. arXiv:2602.18550.
population_categories: Demographic groups (not detailed in abstract)
manipulation: Constructed comparable resumes with known ground-truth superiority
outcome: Ranking validity; abstention; group selection rates
main_result: Many models fail to consistently pick the more qualified resume; do not reliably abstain when candidates are equally qualified; select groups at different rates, sometimes favouring marginalised groups
relation_to_project: Supports a manipulation check that models distinguish our qualification tiers (positive control) and pre-registering tie/abstention handling in forced choice

full_citation: Pavlopoulos, V. (2026). Minimal but conditional: Auditing demographic bias in large language model resume evaluation across commercial and open-weight models. Analytics, 5(3), 30.
population_categories: Gender, race (plus age-related artefact)
manipulation: Reference-anchored comparison against a fixed neutral reference resume; provocation conditions (weaker candidates, relaxed prompt, culture-fit language)
main_result: Gender and race effects negligible under all conditions (equivalence tests vs a justified smallest effect of interest; FDR control; mixed-effects models for clustered repeated evaluations); a seniority positive control confirmed sensitivity; the open-weight model reacted to a few explicit minority-status signals
relation_to_project: Design template: positive control (our qualification tiers), equivalence testing so nulls are informative, mixed models for repeated evaluations; explicit signals matter for open-weight models (our main compute)

full_citation: Yin, L., Alba, D., & Nicoletti, L. (2024, March). OpenAI's GPT is a recruiter's dream tool. Tests show there's racial bias. Bloomberg (data journalism).
population_categories: US; race x gender via names from voter/Census data
manipulation: Ranking of eight near-identical resumes across hundreds of names for four jobs (per README)
main_result: Not verified from the article (paywalled/403); headline claims racial bias in GPT resume ranking
limitations: Journalism; article text not read; byline confirmed via secondary pages only
relation_to_project: Context for public salience of LLM hiring audits; cite only as journalism

full_citation: Yin, H., Vardi, S., & Choudhary, V. (2026). Fragile preferences: A deep dive into order effects in large language models. PNAS Nexus, 5(8), pgag246.
population_categories: not applicable (position effects); name bias noted
manipulation: Order of options in resume comparisons and colour choices
main_result: Strong order effects that depend on quality: first option favoured when all options are high quality, later options when quality is lower; a name bias beyond demographic signals; order effects can make models choose strictly inferior options; temperature-based mitigation
relation_to_project: Position bias may interact with our qualification tier: model order x tier; quads cancel position within quad

full_citation: Wang, P., Li, L., Chen, L., Cai, Z., Zhu, D., Lin, B., Cao, Y., Kong, L., Liu, Q., Liu, T., & Sui, Z. (2024). Large language models are not fair evaluators. In Proceedings of ACL 2024 (Volume 1: Long Papers), 9440-9450.
population_categories: not applicable
manipulation: Order of candidate responses in LLM-as-judge prompts
main_result: Rankings can be flipped by order alone (Vicuna-13B beat ChatGPT on 66 of 80 queries with ChatGPT as evaluator); Balanced Position Calibration aggregates across orders
relation_to_project: Supports presenting every pair in both orders and aggregating

full_citation: Zheng, L., Chiang, W.-L., Sheng, Y., Zhuang, S., Wu, Z., Zhuang, Y., Lin, Z., Li, Z., Li, D., Xing, E., Zhang, H., Gonzalez, J., & Stoica, I. (2023). Judging LLM-as-a-judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36 (Datasets and Benchmarks), 46595-46623.
population_categories: not applicable
manipulation: Position, verbosity, self-enhancement probes in LLM-as-judge
main_result: Documents position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases of LLM judges and mitigation; strong judges reach >80% agreement with humans
relation_to_project: General warrant that pairwise LLM judgements carry position bias

full_citation: Vohra, S., & Ravikiran, M. (2026). The audit decides the verdict: Instrument effects rival demographic bias in LLM decision audits. arXiv:2609.09048 (REALM 2026 workshop at EMNLP 2026).
venue: arXiv preprint (states acceptance at REALM 2026 @ EMNLP 2026)
models_or_system: Five current models (incl. Claude, Gemini, Qwen3.5 open-weight)
population_categories: Race (names) in hiring, lending, medical triage
manipulation: Applicant name only; rating vs ranking vs decide formats; transparent vs camouflaged audits; placebo (hobby) contrasts
main_result: Pre-registered primary test: none of 36 contrasts survives correction; models recognise transparent audits (100% under a forced-choice probe, 89% unprompted) and tie every identical-content comparison, whether the varying detail is race or a hobby; first-listed candidates gain 0.11 rank positions, comparable to the largest demographic effect; temperature 0 is not deterministic
relation_to_project: Supports pairing different base CVs (not identical content) in forced choice to avoid trivial ties and audit recognition; report results per instrument; treat position as a pre-registered design check

full_citation: Chen, Q., & Xiao, Y. (2026). Beyond the name: Demographic leakage in de-identified resumes and evaluation artifacts in LLM bias audits. arXiv:2609.16501.
population_categories: Australia; Anglo, First Nations, Chinese, Indian, Vietnamese; three cue-salience tiers
manipulation: Ethnocultural cues in unstructured prose with language fields held identical; pairwise judge with ties forbidden/neutral/encouraged
outcome: Demographic recoverability; pairwise choice; shortlist and 0-100 score
main_result: Target-group recovery 0.757 overall, 1.000 at high salience; forbidding ties gives an apparent selection-rate ratio of 0.39 with strong position and content effects, permitting ties yields >=94% ties for 7 of 9 models; downstream scores differ very little
relation_to_project: Verdict space drives pairwise results: our forced choice leaves the enum unconstrained, so tie/refusal handling must be pre-registered with a sensitivity analysis

full_citation: Miller, E. (2024). Adding error bars to evals: A statistical approach to language model evaluations. arXiv:2411.00640.
models_or_system: not applicable (statistical method; examples with Anthropic models)
population_categories: not applicable
manipulation: not applicable
main_result: Treat items as draws from a super-population; cluster-adjusted SEs can be up to ~3x naive SEs in real evals; resampling answers K times reduces within-item variance with diminishing returns; analyse paired differences and next-token probabilities
limitations: Preprint; not about bias audits specifically
relation_to_project: Direct warrant that our R repetitions are within-stimulus replicates: cluster by base CV/stimulus (or random effects), analyse paired within-CV contrasts

full_citation: Atil, B., Aykent, S., Chittams, A., Fu, L., Passonneau, R. J., Radcliffe, E., Rajagopal, G. R., Sloan, A., Tudrej, T., Ture, F., Wu, Z., Xu, L., & Baldwin, B. (2024). Non-determinism of 'deterministic' LLM settings. arXiv:2408.04667.
population_categories: not applicable
manipulation: Repeated runs (10) under settings expected to be deterministic
main_result: Accuracy varies up to 15% across runs; best-worst gap up to 70%; no model gives repeatable accuracy across all tasks
relation_to_project: Temperature 0 does not remove run-to-run variance: supports T=0.7 with logged seeds and R repetitions, plus exact model/version logging

full_citation: Kline, P., Rose, E. K., & Walters, C. R. (2022). Systemic discrimination among large U.S. employers. The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 137(4), 1963-2036.
population_categories: US; race (Black/White names), gender
manipulation: Randomised applicant characteristics on fictitious applications
sample_size: >83,000 applications to jobs at 108 large employers
main_result: Black names reduce contact by 2.1 pp; between-company SD of racial gap 1.9 pp; FDR control at 5% identifies 23 discriminating companies
relation_to_project: Methodological analogue for heterogeneity across many units (firms <-> nationalities): variance components plus FDR-controlled unit-level inference

full_citation: Kline, P., Rose, E. K., & Walters, C. R. (2024). A discrimination report card. American Economic Review, 114(8), 2472-2525.
population_categories: US; race, gender
manipulation: Correspondence experiment
main_result: Empirical Bayes ranking procedure assigning ordinal grades to noisy estimates, trading off informativeness against ranking errors
relation_to_project: Template for ranking 22 nationalities with shrinkage and explicit uncertainty instead of over-reading raw ranks

full_citation: Hurlbert, S. H. (1984). Pseudoreplication and the design of ecological field experiments. Ecological Monographs, 54(2), 187-211.
population_categories: not applicable
manipulation: not applicable
main_result: Classic reference defining pseudoreplication (content not re-read here)
relation_to_project: Canonical citation for treating repeated LLM calls on one stimulus as non-independent

full_citation: Bertrand, M., & Mullainathan, S. (2004). Are Emily and Greg more employable than Lakisha and Jamal? A field experiment on labor market discrimination. American Economic Review, 94(4), 991-1013.
population_categories: US; race via names
manipulation: Race-signalling names on resumes
main_result: Foundational name-based correspondence study (content not re-read here)
relation_to_project: Origin of the name-manipulation paradigm most LLM audits copy; we instead manipulate an explicit field

full_citation: Koopmans, R., Veit, S., & Yemane, R. (2019). Taste or statistics? A correspondence study of ethnic, racial and religious labour market discrimination in Germany. Ethnic and Racial Studies, 42(16), 233-252.
models_or_system: HUMAN employers (field experiment, GEMM German arm)
population_categories: Germany; German-born applicants from 35 ethnic groups (34 origin countries + German), incl. Arab-origin groups such as Egyptian, Iraqi, Moroccan; phenotype (white/black/Asian); religion
manipulation: Names typical for the group plus a second mother tongue on the CV; photos for phenotype; religion via volunteering association
sample_size: almost 6,000 vacancies; 8 occupations; ~100 applications per small group (German and Turkish each a quarter of the sample)
main_result: Callback 60% for German-origin vs 47% for Turkish-origin; several groups below Turkish incl. Iraqi and Moroccan (Albanian lowest, 41%); baseline model: Turkish -9 pp, other non-German -5 pp, black -7 pp, Muslim -7 pp; cultural value distance explains group differences better than group education (taste over statistics)
limitations: Small n per group, so the authors do not estimate single-group effects except Turkish; applicants German-born
relation_to_project: Human precedent for origin-level heterogeneity in Germany, incl. several Arab origins, and a theory (value distance) that predicts origin differences; our LLM design can afford large n per origin, which the human study could not
novelty_threat_reason: Human multi-origin German audit; frames within-Arab heterogeneity as an established human question, so our novelty must be framed as LLM-specific

full_citation: Lancee, B. (2021). Ethnic discrimination in hiring: Comparing groups across contexts. Results from a cross-national field experiment. Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies, 47(6), 1181-1200.
venue: Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies
population_categories: 53 ethnic minority groups; Germany, Norway, Netherlands, Spain, UK, US
manipulation: Harmonised fictitious applications
main_result: Introduces the harmonised GEMM study and the methodological challenges of cross-national, multi-group field experiments
relation_to_project: Source of multi-group human benchmarks; model for harmonised multi-origin comparison

full_citation: Di Stasio, V., Lancee, B., Veit, S., & Yemane, R. (2021). Muslim by default or religious discrimination? Results from a cross-national field experiment on hiring discrimination. Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies, 47(6), 1305-1326.
venue: Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies
population_categories: Germany, Netherlands, Norway, Spain, UK; 15 origin countries with sizeable Muslim populations, MENA subset: Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Morocco, Turkey
manipulation: Origin via name, mother tongue on CV and a cover-letter sentence; religion via Muslim vs neutral volunteering association; applicants born or raised in destination
sample_size: not recorded here (see Table 1 of paper)
main_result: 'Muslim by default' penalty (origin from Muslim-majority country without religious signal) significant in all countries except Spain; disclosed Muslim affiliation adds further penalty; origin- and religion-based discrimination contribute independently
limitations: Uneven group sizes; religion signalled only via volunteering
relation_to_project: Nationality from an Arab state can trigger a 'Muslim by default' inference: our total-effect estimand includes it; mechanism claims stay exploratory

full_citation: Di Stasio, V., & de Vries, A. M. (2024). Same religion, different treatment. The role of origin country characteristics in employers' decisions to hire Muslims. Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies, 50(10), 2444-2467.
venue: Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies
population_categories: Britain, Germany, Netherlands, Norway, Spain; Muslim applicants with ancestry from 22 origin countries
manipulation: Harmonised correspondence test; origin-country characteristics as predictors (authoritarianism, gender inequality, conflict/oppression)
main_result: Lower callbacks for Muslims the higher the authoritarianism and gender inequality of their origin country; authoritarianism most robust; association significant only for men
limitations: Abstract only; list of the 22 countries not verified
relation_to_project: Closest human analogue of our core question: origin-level heterogeneity within a broad category explained by origin-country traits; supplies pre-registrable moderators (e.g., authoritarianism, gender inequality) for exploratory analysis across the 22 Arab origins
